name: Bash
summary: Write scripts that preserve filenames, inspect exit status, read lines, and manage temporary output.

prerequisites: Know how to save a plain text file.
Run examples with bash lesson.sh from a terminal. The temporary-file example uses Unix mktemp, rm, and rmdir. Windows users need a Bash environment with these commands.
metadata.miniProject: Build a reading-list report from a text file. Keep filenames quoted, skip blank or comment lines, and report a nonzero status for missing input. Test with a path that contains spaces.

lessons.title: Quote paths and preserve arguments
lessons.explanation: Double quotes keep spaces in an expanded value together. Single quotes make the text inside them literal. In a script or function, "$@" expands to the original arguments as separate words.
lessons.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
name='study notes.txt'
set -- "$name" 'lab notes.txt'
printf 'count: %s\n' "$#"
for argument in "$@"; do
    printf '<%s>\n' "$argument"
done

api.description: Forward every original argument without merging it with its neighbors.
Read the number of positional arguments.

api.name: printf
api.description: Write values using an explicit format.

lessons.practice: Set three arguments, including one with spaces and one containing an asterisk. Print each argument between brackets.
lessons.pitfall: An unquoted expansion can split a filename into words and interpret glob characters.

exercise.expected: Preserve each argument exactly as written.
exercise.completion: There are three output lines, and the asterisk remains a literal character.

lessons.title: Exit status, tests, and functions
lessons.explanation: A command reports zero for success and a nonzero status otherwise. The if condition executes a command and inspects that status. A shell function can use return to send a status to its caller.
lessons.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
report() {
    if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
        return 2
    fi
    printf 'ready: %s\n' "$1"
}

report 'study notes'
if report; then
    printf 'ready\n'
else
    printf 'status: %s\n' "$?"
fi

api.name: test / [ ]
api.description: Check a condition. Leave spaces around the opening and closing tokens.

api.name: return
api.description: Finish a function and set its status.
Read the status of the immediately preceding command.

lessons.practice: Write a function that prints its first argument only if the argument contains text. Use status 2 otherwise.
lessons.pitfall: Read $? before running another command. A later command replaces the status.

exercise.expected: Distinguish valid input from a missing or empty first argument.
exercise.completion: A nonempty argument prints once. Both no argument and an empty argument return status 2.

lessons.title: Keep filenames in an indexed array
lessons.explanation: A Bash indexed array holds separate strings under numeric indices. Append elements with +=(...). Quote the all-elements expansion so every original value stays a separate argument.
lessons.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tasks=('read chapter' 'review notes')
tasks+=('run samples')
printf 'tasks: %s\n' "${#tasks[@]}"
printf '%s\n' "${tasks[@]}"

api.name: array=(...)
api.description: Create an indexed array with one element per quoted value.

api.name: array+=(...)
api.description: Append elements to an indexed array.

api.name: ${array[@]}
api.description: Expand all indexed values. Put the expansion in double quotes.

lessons.practice: Store two filenames, append a third, and print the first and last values separately.
lessons.pitfall: Bash arrays are a Bash feature. Running the example as sh can fail.
lessons.expectedOutput:
tasks: 3
read chapter
review notes
run samples

exercise.expected: Use an indexed array for filenames containing spaces.
exercise.completion: Changing the filenames changes the printed values without splitting a path.

lessons.title: Read complete lines safely
lessons.explanation: The read builtin stores input in a variable. IFS= keeps leading and trailing whitespace. The -r option preserves literal backslashes. Redirect the input to the loop when it should read a file or here-document.
lessons.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while IFS= read -r row; do
    case "$row" in
        ''|\#*) continue ;;
    esac
    printf '<%s>\n' "$row"
done <<'DATA'
# examples
  first item
path\example

DATA

api.name: IFS= read -r
api.description: Read one line without trimming whitespace or interpreting backslashes.

api.name: <<'DATA'
api.description: Supply literal multi-line input with a quoted delimiter.

lessons.practice: Skip blank and comment lines in a reading list. Print each remaining line with a number while preserving its spacing.
lessons.pitfall: An unterminated last line can set the variable while read returns failure. Handle that case explicitly if your input may lack a final newline.

exercise.expected: Print a numbered list of data lines.
exercise.completion: Comments and empty lines do not consume a number. A line beginning with two spaces retains them.

lessons.title: Create and clean up temporary output
lessons.explanation: A temporary directory gives each run its own output location. Check that creation succeeds. Register cleanup once you have the directory, then quote every use of the generated path.
lessons.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
folder=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
cleanup() {
    if [ -f "$folder/report.txt" ]; then
        rm -- "$folder/report.txt"
    fi
    rmdir -- "$folder"
}
trap cleanup EXIT

printf 'items: 3\n' > "$folder/report.txt" || exit 1
while IFS= read -r line; do
    printf 'report: %s\n' "$line"
done < "$folder/report.txt"

api.name: $(command)
api.description: Use the output of a command as a value.

api.name: trap cleanup EXIT
api.description: Run a cleanup function when this shell exits.
Open the destination for output, replacing its existing contents.

lessons.practice: Write two report lines into a temporary file, read them back, and check that the directory disappears after the script exits.
lessons.pitfall: A fixed path such as /tmp/report.txt can collide with another run. Give each run its own directory.

exercise.expected: Keep temporary output private to the run and remove the files you created.
exercise.completion: Two consecutive runs produce the same output and leave no temporary report files.
